facts.statement: Segnosaurus lived in southeastern Mongolia during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 102 to 86 million years ago.
facts.quote: Segnosaurus is a genus of therizinosaurid dinosaur that lived in what is now southeastern Mongolia during the Late Cretaceous, about 102–86 million years ago.

facts.statement: Multiple incomplete but well-preserved specimens of Segnosaurus were discovered in the Gobi Desert in the 1970s, and the species was named in 1979.
facts.quote: Multiple incomplete but well-preserved specimens were discovered in the Gobi Desert in the 1970s, and in 1979 the genus and species Segnosaurus galbinensis were named.

facts.statement: A joint Soviet-Mongolian expedition discovered the partial skeleton of Segnosaurus at the Amtgay locality in 1973.
facts.quote: In 1973, a joint Soviet–Mongolian expedition investigating the Bayan Shireh Formation at the Amtgay locality in the Gobi Desert of southeastern Mongolia discovered fossils that included the partial skeleton of an unknown dinosaur.

facts.statement: The genus and species Segnosaurus galbinensis were named by paleontologist Altangerel Perle in 1979.
facts.quote: These fossils were scientifically described in 1979 by the paleontologist Altangerel Perle, who named the new genus and species Segnosaurus galbiensis.

facts.statement: The generic name Segnosaurus means "slow lizard", derived from Latin and Ancient Greek roots.
facts.quote: The generic name is derived from the Latin word segnis ("slow") and the Ancient Greek sauros ("lizard").

facts.statement: Segnosaurus was estimated to be about 6 to 7 meters long and weigh approximately 1.3 metric tons.
facts.quote: Segnosaurus was a large-bodied therizinosaur that is estimated to have been about 6–7 m long and to have weighed about 1.3 MT.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus was a bipedal dinosaur with its body trunk tilted upwards.
facts.quote: It would have been bipedal, with the trunk of its body tilted upwards.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus had a small head with a beak and a long, slender neck.
facts.quote: The head was small with a beak at the tip of the jaws, and the neck was long and slender.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus had robust forelimbs with three fingers bearing large claws and four-toed feet.
facts.quote: The forelimbs were robust and had three fingers which bore large claws, and the feet had four toes supporting the foot—apart from therizinosaurs, all theropods had three-toed feet.

facts.statement: The lower jaw of Segnosaurus was down-turned at the front, and its teeth featured additional denticles and third cutting edges on some hindmost teeth.
facts.quote: The lower jaw was down-turned at the front and the teeth were distinct in having additional denticles as well as third cutting edges in some of the hindmost teeth.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus had a backwards-turned pubic bone, a feature shared only with birds and their closest dinosaur relatives.
facts.quote: The pubic bone was turned backwards, a feature that is only seen in birds and the dinosaurs most closely related to them.

facts.statement: Therizinosaurs like Segnosaurus likely used their long forelimbs, necks, and beaks for browsing and had large guts for processing food.
facts.quote: Therizinosaurs probably used their long forelimbs, long necks, and beaks when browsing, and large guts for processing food.

facts.statement: The family Segnosauridae is considered a junior synonym of the family Therizinosauridae.
facts.quote: The new fossils also showed Segnosauridae was a junior synonym of the earlier named family Therizinosauridae.

facts.statement: A 2020 study by Campione and Evans calculated the body mass of Segnosaurus at 4.17 metric tons.
facts.quote: Campione & Evans in 2020, however, calculated its body mass at 4.17 MT.

facts.statement: Therizinosaurs are known to have possessed simple, primitive feathers, as evidenced by fossils in genera like Beipiaosaurus and Jianchangosaurus.
facts.quote: Therizinosaurs are known to have had simple, primitive feathers as evidenced by fossils of the basal (or "primitive") genera Beipiaosaurus—the second-known non-bird dinosaur preserved with such integuments after Sinosauropteryx—and Jianchangosaurus.

facts.statement: It is debated how widespread the distinguishing anatomical features of Segnosaurus are among therizinosaurs due to incomplete preservation in most genera.
facts.quote: Since most therizinosaurs are incompletely known, it is uncertain how many of the anatomical features that are used to distinguish Segnosaurus are widespread among the group; many genera cannot be directly compared because the equivalent bones are not preserved.

facts.statement: The nearly complete right half of the Segnosaurus lower jaw is 379 mm long, 55.5 mm high, and 24.5 mm deep.
facts.quote: The nearly complete right hemimandible (half of the mandible) is 379 mm long from front to back, 55.5 mm at the highest point, and 24.5 mm at the lowest.

facts.statement: The front part of the Segnosaurus lower jaw is deflected downwards at a unique 30-degree angle.
facts.quote: The front-most part of the dentary was strongly deflected downwards at about a 30-degree angle, a unique feature for this genus.

facts.statement: The toothless front section of the Segnosaurus lower jaw measures 25.5 mm in length on the holotype specimen.
facts.quote: The expansive, toothless front region of the dentary spans 25.5 mm on the right hemimandible of the holotype.

facts.statement: The toothless portion of the Segnosaurus lower jaw is 20% of the total tooth row, which is 150.3 mm long.
facts.quote: Proportionally, the toothless part of the dentary is 20% of its tooth row, which is 150.3 mm long.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus is distinct among therizinosaurs because the rear part of its lower jaw has no teeth.
facts.quote: Segnosaurus was distinct among therizinosaurs in that the hindmost part of the dentary was toothless.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus had 24 tooth sockets in the front two-thirds of its lower jaw, whereas Erlikosaurus had 31 sockets along nearly the entire jaw.
facts.quote: The teeth were restricted to the front two-thirds of the dentary, which bore 24 alveoli (tooth sockets) in a manner similar to Jianchangosaurus but different from Erlikosaurus, in which nearly the entire dentary was toothed, bearing 31 alveoli.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus possesses the fewest teeth in the lower jaw among therizinosaurs, with 24 per side, and has the largest teeth known for the group.
facts.quote: Segnosaurus had the fewest teeth in the dentary; 24 in each half determined from the number of sockets, as well as the largest teeth known among therizinosaurs.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus teeth are leaf-shaped with tall, sideways-compressed crowns that have slightly recurved tips.
facts.quote: The dentary teeth were foliodont (leaf-shaped) and bore enlarged, relatively tall, sideways compressed crowns with a slight recurvature at the upper margin of the tips.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus teeth have large, bulbous serrations with about 5 to 6 per 3 mm that get smaller toward the tips.
facts.quote: The denticles (serrations) were large and bulbous, diminishing slightly in size towards the tooth tips, with about 5–6 denticles per 3 mm.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus is unique among all known theropods for having triple cutting edges on its teeth.
facts.quote: Segnosaurus was unique among all known theropods in possessing triple carinae.

facts.statement: The 22nd and 23rd lower jaw teeth of Segnosaurus are significantly smaller than the others and possess an additional third cutting edge with serrations on their inner sides.
facts.quote: The 22nd and 23rd dentary teeth of Segnosaurus were significantly smaller than the rest, almost conidont, and had an additional third carina with denticles on their inner sides.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus replaced its teeth in waves moving from the back to the front of the jaws, involving two to three erupting teeth at a time.
facts.quote: Segnosaurus replaced its teeth in waves running from back to front of the jaws, that encompassed two to three erupting crowns.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the bone growth over the 14th tooth socket in the right jaw of the holotype was caused by injury or disease, as the teeth in that area are too damaged to assess the effect.
facts.quote: The 14th alveolus on the right dentary of the holotype is walled over by seemingly pathological (due to injury or disease) bone growth but the teeth in that part of the dentary are damaged so it is not possible to determine how the teeth were affected by this.

facts.statement: Researchers cannot conclude whether the triple cutting edges on the left jaw teeth are a normal feature or a result of pathology, unlike the right jaw which shows signs of injury or disease.
facts.quote: Segnosaurus was unique among all known theropods in possessing triple carinae. The 14th alveolus on the right dentary of the holotype is walled over by seemingly pathological (due to injury or disease) bone growth but the teeth in that part of the dentary are damaged so it is not possible to determine how the teeth were affected by this. The teeth in the same area of the left dentary bear triple carinae, though this dentary has no external indications of pathology that could have led to this condition, thus it cannot be concluded nor ruled out that this feature is the result of a pathology.

facts.statement: The humerus of Segnosaurus measured 560 mm in length.
facts.quote: The massive humerus was 560 mm in length

facts.statement: The radius of Segnosaurus was massive, measuring about 60 percent of the humerus length, and had a straight shaft.
facts.quote: The radius was also massive—about 60 percent of the humerus—with a straight shaft.

facts.statement: The ulna of Segnosaurus was thicker than the radius, slightly longer at about 70 percent of the humerus length, and slightly twisted along its middle axis.
facts.quote: The ulna was thicker than the radius and slightly longer—about 70 percent of the humerus—and slightly twisted along its middle axis.

facts.statement: The hand of Segnosaurus was tridactyl, meaning it had three fingers.
facts.quote: The hand was tridactyl (three-fingered).

facts.statement: The pelvis of Segnosaurus was robust and featured sharply sideways-directed lobes at the front.
facts.quote: The pelvis of Segnosaurus was robust and had sharply sideways-directed lobes at the front.

facts.statement: The pubic bone of Segnosaurus was directed backwards and down parallel to the ischium, a condition known as opisthopubic.
facts.quote: The pubic bone was directed backwards and down in parallel with the ischium; this backwards orientation of the pubic bone is known as the opisthopubic condition.

facts.statement: The femur of Segnosaurus was straight with an oval cross-section and measured 840 mm in length.
facts.quote: The femur was straight with an oval cross-section and was 840 mm in length.

facts.statement: The epiphyses on the upper metatarsals of Segnosaurus were enlarged, a distinctive feature of the genus.
facts.quote: The epiphyses on the upper metatarsals were hypertrophied (enlarged), a distinctive feature of the genus.

facts.statement: The sacrum of Segnosaurus consisted of six firmly fused vertebrae.
facts.quote: The sacrum consisted of six, firmly fused vertebrae

facts.statement: It is debated whether the pelvic similarities between Segnosaurus and Nothronychus result from a shared common ancestor exclusive to derived therizinosaurids or from the retention of basal features lost in other relatives.
facts.quote: Some features of the pelvis were similar to that of Nothronychus, particularly the ischia, but it is uncertain whether these similarities were due to them having a common ancestor to the exclusion of other derived therizinosaurids, or because they retained basal features since lost in other relatives.

facts.statement: The forelimb elements of Therizinosaurus were originally thought to belong to a giant turtle when they were described in 1954.
facts.quote: the forelimb elements of Therizinosaurus itself were originally identified as belonging to a giant turtle when described in 1954

facts.statement: Perle tentatively classified Segnosauridae as theropods based on similarities in the mandible and front teeth.
facts.quote: He tentatively classified Segnosauridae as theropods, traditionally thought of as the "meat-eating" dinosaurs, pointing to similarities in the mandible and its front teeth.

facts.statement: Perle suggested that Segnosaurus and Therizinosaurus belonged in a family to the exclusion of Deinocheiridae.
facts.quote: Perle to suggest they belonged in a family to the exclusion of Deinocheiridae

facts.statement: In 1984, Gregory S. Paul concluded that segnosaurs were derived, late-surviving Cretaceous prosauropods with no theropodan features.
facts.quote: Gregory S. Paul concluded in 1984 that segnosaurs had no theropodan features but were derived, late-surviving Cretaceous prosauropods

facts.statement: In 1986, Jacques Gauthier concluded that segnosaurs were prosauropods.
facts.quote: In a 1986 study of the inter-relationships of saurischian dinosaurs, Jacques Gauthier concluded segnosaurs were prosauropods.
